title: Describing several things: plural adjective
summary: When describing ordinary plural items individually after ovat (“are”), use a plural partitive adjective: Autot ovat uusia. — The cars are new.
objectives: Choose a plural partitive adjective when describing individual ordinary plural items after ovat.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: When describing the individual members of an ordinary plural group after ovat (“are”), use a plural partitive adjective. The subject noun remains plural nominative, the form naming the things.

An adjective after the verb describes what the subject is like. This job is called a predicate adjective. It differs from an adjective placed directly before a noun. Here the complete subject forms, ovat and adjective choices are supplied, so the scored Finnish task is choosing case and number.

The examples describe separate ordinary items individually. Plural-only nouns and a group described as one whole have other patterns; this lesson does not generalize its rule to them. Negation does not automatically make every describing adjective partitive.
keyPoints: Keep the supplied plural subject and ovat; choose the plural partitive adjective for this individual-description meaning.

steps: When describing the individual members of an ordinary plural group after ovat (“are”), use a plural partitive adjective. The subject noun remains plural nominative, the form naming the things.
Autot means “cars” and works as the plural nominative noun used as the subject. Add -t to auto: autot.
ovat means “are” and works as the verb agreeing with the plural subject. ovat is the present third-person plural of olla (“to be”). The supplied verb agrees with the plural subject.
uusia means “new” and works as the plural partitive adjective describing each thing. Keep dictionary-form uusi and add -a: uusia.

commonMistakes: The plural subject keeps its nominative form; the adjective has a different job and case.
Do not choose a singular partitive adjective for these several-things descriptions.
A whole-group description or a plural-only noun needs separate teaching.
